source.title: TwinBreak: Jailbreaking LLM Security Alignments based on Twin Prompts
source.authors: T. Krauß; Hamid Dashtbani; Alexandra Dmitrienko

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether safety behavior can be removed by targeted parameter pruning, a different intervention from the listed original sources.
record.gate_note: The paper tests targeted parameter pruning and reports harmful-response evaluation results, bearing on V5. It does not test harmful or benign fine-tuning, aligned-versus-base per-token KL, compliant-prefix/suffix/decoding bypasses, or methods for deepening safety. Its statements about switching to the unpruned model after 50 generated tokens are part of the pruning procedure, not a standalone test of compliant prefilling. Discussion of fine-tuning and suffix attacks cites other work and is not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: TwinBreak prunes a small set of MLP Gate/Up parameters (about 1% per round, five rounds) and measures harmful-response ASR. That bears on V5, whether a small set of weights carries safety behaviour. The pruning method differs from the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is roughly right. The authors conclude that TwinBreak removes safety alignment through targeted iterative pruning, with ASR of 89-98% and little utility loss, and that the safety mechanism is localized in a small, sparse parameter set. They also report that no existing defense is embedded in the parameters and suggest spreading safety more broadly as future work. One correction: the 50-token pruned-then-unpruned generation is an optional step for protecting utility.
record.recipe_differences: This study uses twin-prompt activation comparisons to identify and iteratively prune selected parameters. It does not use fine-tuning or measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL. The intervention is parameter removal, targeting Gate and Up MLP layers.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with model, evaluation dataset, pruning iteration/rate, targeted layers, utility-parameter retention, dataset size, activation-token choice, and the number of response tokens generated by the pruned model. The paper reports that full-batch use of non-twin prompts reduces ASR and/or utility, and that single versus multiple pruning iterations changes the ASR-utility trade-off.
record.problems: The authors note that LlamaGuard3 can produce false positives and false negatives and may overemphasize refusal keywords rather than response detail. Utility effects vary by model and task; some configurations cause large utility losses or incoherent outputs. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many additional combinations of pruning dataset size, hyperparameters, utility benchmarks, model families, and comparisons with other methods. Rows were limited to principal harmful-response results across the main evaluation datasets, the StrongREJECT results, and selected target-layer comparisons; additional dataset-size tables 11–14, utility benchmark tables 15–20 and 24–25, and related-method comparison tables 7, 21–23 were not exhaustively extracted. Cited results from other work were excluded.

untested.parts: Per-token KL between aligned and base models is not tested.
Prefilling, suffix and decoding bypasses are not tested. The 50-token pruned-then-unpruned generation is part of the pruning procedure.
Causes of shallowness in data or objective are not tested.
Deepening training is not tested. The authors only suggest distributing safety more broadly as future work.

missing.what: ASR for the Gate+Up+Down configuration and the all-layers and attention-pruning ablations, plus the single 5%-pass, 10-iteration and non-twin-prompt variants
Larger-model and cross-family StrongREJECT scores for TwinBreak across 16 models (unpruned 0.057 average vs 0.744), and the comparison with directional ablation
LLaMA 3.1 and Qwen 2.5 reach high ASR at lower pruning rates (0.1% and 0.2% per iteration), which suggests very sparse safety parameters
Utility cost of pruning (about -1.2% HellaSwag on average, with larger drops on some models and tasks)

record.verdict_notes: Several rows mix up their roles. Controls (unpruned references) carry V5 links and some carry a 'partial' state. Rows r50 and r51 compare inference procedures with a wrong model subject (r50 is Qwen 2.5 32B, not LLaMA 2 7B), and r45-r49 are ablations of the study's own method. The verdict rests on the main-table rows, which come from a single run each, with no uncertainty reported. The ASR judge is LlamaGuard3, which the authors note over-weights refusal keywords.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning on few to a few hundred examples.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Aligned-versus-base per-token KL across response positions.
Compliant prefilling, suffixes, and decoding changes as bypasses.
The study prunes a targeted subset of parameters, but does not establish that safety is exclusively or generally carried by a small set across alternative interventions.
Whether training data or objective causes safety shallowness.
Training that deepens safety and whether such training holds up.

relationships.condition: TwinBreak pruning of roughly 5% of Gate/Up MLP parameters (excluding first and last layers) on LLaMA 2 7B, LLaMA 3.1 8B, Gemma 2 9B and Qwen 2.5 7B
relationships.reason: Unpruned ASR is 0-18% and pruned ASR reaches 92-99% on HarmBench, AdvBench and JailbreakBench. StrongREJECT scores rise from under 0.08 to 0.68-0.81 (r02-r09, r11-r12, r14-r15, r17-r18, r20-r21, r23-r24, r26-r27, r29-r30, r32-r33, r35-r36, r38, r40, r42, r44). Safety is removable by pruning a small parameter fraction with modest utility loss.
relationships.display_finding: Attack success rose from 0–18% unpruned to 92–99% on HarmBench, AdvBench and JailbreakBench, and StrongREJECT scores rose from under 0.08 to 0.68–0.81, with modest utility loss.
